newsitem.title: UK: Euro bankers cool on EMI reserve requirements.
newsitem.headline: Euro bankers cool on EMI reserve requirements.

text.p: Many European bankers on Friday were quick to criticise a suggestion of a reserve requirement being imposed by a future European Central Bank (ECB), which some said would amount to a tax on the sector.

"The imposition of reserve requirements is unnecessary for the efficient conduct of monetary policy and threatens to distort the market," Tim Sweeney, director general of the British Bankers Association (BBA), said in a statement. Earlier the European Monetary Institute (EMI) revealed details of the monetary policy instruments for the future central bank, but made clear final decisions on several key outstanding issues would have to be made by the ECB itself.
The new central bank, which will take over monetary policy responsibility as soon as the European single currency is launched in 1999, will not be up and running until 1998.

The BBA, which represents more than 300 British and overseas banks active in Britain, was joined by many of its European counterparts in expressing disappointment that the EMI is still lokking at the possibility of minimum reserves.
Reserve requirements are the percentage of bank deposits that firms must set aside with their central bank. Lowering or raising this requirement effectively influences money supply.
Sweeney said such a move would also lead to business moving away from the area covered by the euro, while his Luxembourg counterpart Lucien Thiel said it may lead to a two-tier system.

"If (the ECB) insists on minimum reserves within the euro zone that don't pay interest, and the City of London does not have minimum reserves -- or does and pays interest, London will become an offshore euro centre," Thiel said.
According to the Federal Association of German Banks, which represents private sector banks in Germany where a reserve requirement is currrently in force, called the mechanism superfluous.
The German bankers also said it would be harmful to financial centres in the future euro currency area and would make it harder for the ECB to conduct monetary policy.

Other industry associations expressed similar views, the French banking association suggesting if requirements were imposed, they should bear interest. And the Bank of England (BoE) said it argued against reserve requirements on the basis they imposed a tax on the institutions covered by them.

The BoE also said reserve requirements were inferior to market approaches, which could be used for the same ends. But French monetary authorities, believed to be keen on the idea of using minimum reserves to control money market volatility, argue that without them an ECB would be obliged to conduct daily "fine tuning" operations of the type currently carried out by the Bank of England to smooth volatility in money market rates.

The EMI did not specify which firms would be subject to a reserve, merely saying that in considering the efficiency of a such a system, the ECB "might need to impose reserve ratios on a broad range of liabilities and institutions".

It said it needed to study further the extension of the definition in the relevant article "so as to allow the ECB to subject a broader range of financial institutions than credit institutions alone to reserve requirements".
The terms and conditions of any such system would be uniform throughout the area covered by a single currency, it said.

Minimum reserves already bear no interest in Finland and Germany. But the Bank of Finland's deposit requirements have been moderate and the system has worked well, according to Sirpa Wallius, economist at Finland's largest banking group Merita Oy.
"But if it were up to us (the banks) alone, we would prefer no minimum reserve system at all...it is like a tax on banks," Wallius added.

Banks in both Belgium and Luxembourg, where minimum reserves are not enforced, oppose their introduction. In Luxembourg, where the banking sector has blossomed in part thanks to the fact German banks there could circumvent domestic capital requirements, this is particularly the case.

Dutch banks, which currently earn interest of between 2.0 and 2.5 percent on central bank deposits, said they would prefer this to continue. ABN AMRO said a system of interest-free deposits would place Dutch banks at a disadvantage to rivals in Germany, which has such a system now.
